implementation_notes: Go's func values capture by reference to the variables they name, and Go's loop variables were shared across iterations until language version 1.22 (per-iteration scoping declared by the go directive in go.mod). Writing go 1.22 or later in go.mod, or re-binding 'v := v' inside the loop, makes each closure capture its own variable. Go has no closures over mutable state beyond plain variables, and every closure escapes to the heap if it outlives the frame, which the escape analysis decides for you - check it with -gcflags=-m.
idiom_name: function literal capturing variables by reference; per-iteration loop variables since go 1.22
pitfalls: Before Go 1.22 every closure in a loop captured the same variable; the re-binding idiom is harmless but redundant on modern toolchains.
Escaping to the heap: a closure returned or passed to a goroutine is heap-allocated, so a closure per iteration in a hot loop costs an allocation per iteration.
Capturing a loop variable and mutating it inside the closure gives every instance the same storage - the classic 'all handlers see the last value' bug.
